knowledge_point.title: Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Trigonometric Functions

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral. Give an exact answer.

$$
\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{6}} \frac{7}{\sqrt{1 - 9 x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the linear substitution $u=3 x.$ Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=3,\qquad \mathrm{d}x=(\frac{1}{3})\,\mathrm{d}u.
$$

Change both bounds using the same substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=0&\Longrightarrow u=(3)(0)=0 \\ x=\frac{1}{6}&\Longrightarrow u=(3)(\frac{1}{6})=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Both transformed endpoints lie strictly between $-1$ and $1$, so the integrand is continuous throughout the interval.

Apply the basic inverse-trigonometric integral:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \int_{0}^{\frac{1}{6}} \frac{7}{\sqrt{1 - 9 x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= 7\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{6}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(3 x)^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= 7(\frac{1}{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{7}{3}\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{7}{3}[\operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}]_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}} \\  &= \frac{7}{3}(\operatorname{arcsin}(\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}(0)) \\  &= \frac{7}{3}((\frac{\pi}{6})-(0)) \\  &= \frac{7 \pi}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral. Give an exact answer.

$$
\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{6}} \frac{8}{36 x^{2} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the linear substitution $u=6 x.$ Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=6,\qquad \mathrm{d}x=(\frac{1}{6})\,\mathrm{d}u.
$$

Change both bounds using the same substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=0&\Longrightarrow u=(6)(0)=0 \\ x=\frac{1}{6}&\Longrightarrow u=(6)(\frac{1}{6})=1\end{aligned}
$$

Apply the basic inverse-trigonometric integral:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+u^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \int_{0}^{\frac{1}{6}} \frac{8}{36 x^{2} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= 8\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{6}} \frac{1}{1+(6 x)^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= 8(\frac{1}{6})\int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{1+u^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{4}{3}\int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{1+u^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{4}{3}[\operatorname{arctan}{\left(u \right)}]_{0}^{1} \\  &= \frac{4}{3}(\operatorname{arctan}(1)-\operatorname{arctan}(0)) \\  &= \frac{4}{3}((\frac{\pi}{4})-(0)) \\  &= \frac{\pi}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral. Give an exact answer.

$$
\int_{0}^{\frac{2}{9}} \frac{5}{81 x^{2} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

{{coefficient}} $\operatorname{arctan}($ {{argument}} $)$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the linear substitution $u=9 x.$ Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=9,\qquad \mathrm{d}x=(\frac{1}{9})\,\mathrm{d}u.
$$

Change both bounds using the same substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=0&\Longrightarrow u=(9)(0)=0 \\ x=\frac{2}{9}&\Longrightarrow u=(9)(\frac{2}{9})=2\end{aligned}
$$

Apply the basic inverse-trigonometric integral:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+u^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \int_{0}^{\frac{2}{9}} \frac{5}{81 x^{2} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= 5\int_{0}^{\frac{2}{9}} \frac{1}{1+(9 x)^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= 5(\frac{1}{9})\int_{0}^{2} \frac{1}{1+u^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{5}{9}\int_{0}^{2} \frac{1}{1+u^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{5}{9}[\operatorname{arctan}{\left(u \right)}]_{0}^{2} \\  &= \frac{5}{9}(\operatorname{arctan}(2)-\operatorname{arctan}(0)) \\  &= \frac{5}{9}((\operatorname{arctan}{\left(2 \right)})-(0)) \\  &= \frac{5 \operatorname{arctan}{\left(2 \right)}}{9}\end{aligned}
$$
